point: DERs come in three types with different flexibility, are underused, and growing feed-in will need new management beyond fit-and-forget.
Papers integrate DERs in existing balancing or ancillary markets or in new distribution markets, and agree aggregation is needed.
An active DSO enables DER flexibility but demands redesigned TSO-DSO coordination.
Coordination schemes differ mainly in how centralised they are and in the information exchanged between TSO and DSO.
The TSO-managed scheme is closest to today but computationally heavy, though studies find it still improves system performance.
The hybrid central-market scheme is theoretically most efficient but needs heavy communication and causes operator conflict, so it seems unrealistic.
DSO-managed schemes, especially local ancillary markets, need less coordination and preserve information barriers, so they are judged the most promising.
Givisiez et al. identify distributed, hierarchical and centralised optimisation as the three techniques for modelling coordination.
TSO-managed models share centralised optimisation, while DSO-managed models differ more among themselves.
Most DSO-managed models are bi-level hierarchical optimisations, differing in how and when the DSO and TSO sub-problems are handled.
Yuan and Hesamzadeh work in economic dispatch while Savvopoulos operates later on the ancillary market, so their timing differs.
Najibi and Mahboubi-Moghaddam solve the TSO first and then DSOs, iterating on price signals toward a near-optimal solution in dispatch.
Calvillo et al. differ by maximising DER owner and aggregator benefit on the day-ahead market rather than system cost.
Few models place DERs in re-dispatch, and none with a DSO model, so TSO-DSO re-dispatch is unexplored.
Few models include a DSO sub-problem or DER re-dispatch, which defines the gap this paper fills.
The paper contributes coordination frameworks, their optimisation models and a country-wide comparison of re-dispatch from DSO flexibility, which is rare in the literature.
DSO-side flexibility is growing and falls into three technical categories, and this paper looks at its load-shifting potential.
Market design does not yet support this flexibility, so the paper asks which markets suit providers and how to model multi-market bids.
Villar et al. define three flexibility products, so providers can trade in several markets.
Studies agree integration needs better TSO-DSO coordination and matters with more renewables, but disagree on which market to enter.
Several consortia see ancillary markets as best for DSO flexibility and stress an active DSO and aggregators.
Eid, Xu and Villar find more potential in balancing markets while also needing aggregators.
Newman and MacDougall and IRENA find intraday markets exploit flexibility better than real-time balancing, giving liquidity and efficiency gains.
Capacity market use of distributed flexibility improves the system but pays providers enough only with high renewable shares.
Few papers take the provider view, and those that do find aggregation pays and intraday markets beat day-ahead because of higher volatility.
Most work covers one market, yet trading in several markets increases aggregator and provider benefit.
Multi-market bidding research exists but targets conventional producers, so strategies must be adapted to flexibility providers.
Coordinated bidding modestly beats separate bidding and gains weight as price gaps between markets widen.
Coordinated bidding becomes more attractive with more renewables, and stochastic treatment of later-market uncertainty raises revenue over deterministic planning.
Roos and Ottesen pick similar markets, one specific and one general, and both use limited scope and physical detail.
Little literature considers provider benefit and most covers one market, but intraday and capacity markets look valuable for this flexibility.
The paper lets DSO aggregators allocate flexibility between capacity and intraday markets with stochastic intraday prices, at country scale for Germany in 2030.
